title: How many games actually sit behind a bin
subtitle: Within-game autocorrelation, effective sample size, and the game-cluster bootstrap for MLB and international-soccer calibration
abstract: Two published calibration exhibits report reliability bins built from tens of thousands of in-game probability rows, but a row is not a game. Within a single MLB or international-soccer match, the model and market probability paths move smoothly toward one fixed final outcome, so consecutive rows sit close to their neighbor rather than arriving as fresh independent draws. This paper reads three already-published artifacts -- the lag-1 within-game residual-autocorrelation ledger, the effective-sample-size (ESS) ledger it feeds, and the game-cluster bootstrap behind the calibration-stability exhibit -- to state plainly how much independent support a bin's row count carries. In MLB, 78,986 rows across 227 games carry a median model-side lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.9809; the AR(1) approximation puts the effective sample size at 761 rows, and the conservative distinct-game anchor puts it at 227, an 18.7x inflation of the raw row count. In international soccer, 9,003 rows across 51 games show a median autocorrelation of 0.9624, an AR(1) ESS of 172, and a game anchor of 51, a 13.3x inflation. The calibration-stability exhibit already resamples whole games rather than rows to build its 95 percent intervals (1,000 replicates, cluster unit game_id), which is why several MLB market-side bins keep a gap interval that includes zero even with thousands of rows behind them. The reading that follows is descriptive only: n in a bin caption counts rows, not evidence, and the game count is the number that should anchor how much a reader trusts it.

blocks.text: A calibration bin on the published reliability page lists an n, sometimes in the thousands. The question here is what that n is actually made of: how many separate games contributed those rows, whether rows inside one game move independently of each other, and what the effective sample size behind a bin is once that dependence is counted. It also asks why the calibration-stability exhibit already resamples by game rather than by row, and what that choice buys a reader who wants to know how much a bin's gap can be trusted.

This is a read of three artifacts CourtVision has already published, not a new measurement: the lag-1 within-game residual-autocorrelation ledger (residual_autocorrelation.json), the effective-sample-size ledger it feeds (ess_ledger.json), and the game-cluster bootstrap that already sits under the calibration-stability exhibit (calibration_stability.json). No new number is computed here beyond simple ratios of numbers each artifact already reports.

residual_autocorrelation.json records the lag-1 sample autocorrelation of the signed residual (probability minus terminal outcome) for every (game_id, side) series, ordered by timestamp, for MLB and international soccer, on both the model side and the market side. It applies two floors before a series counts: at least 10 rows per game, and a minimum residual variance of 1e-9 (a series with a flat residual has no autocorrelation to measure). MLB contributes 227 usable series across 78,986 rows; international soccer contributes 51 series across 9,003 rows. A third candidate corpus, labelled mlb_clean, is explicitly skipped as a byte-identical duplicate of the mlb corpus, so it never inflates either sport's row or game count.

ess_ledger.json takes that autocorrelation and turns it into an effective-sample-size estimate: an AR(1) approximation (ESS_AR1) and a distinct-game anchor, then reports the minimum of the two as ess_anchor because the AR(1) formula is only a first-order model of a residual path that is, by construction, smooth and terminal-constant -- a stronger form of dependence than a single lag coefficient fully captures.

calibration_stability.json is the reliability exhibit itself: 10 probability bins per sport per side (model and market), each carrying both n (rows) and n_games (distinct games), together with a mean forecast, a mean outcome, and a calibration gap. The interval around that gap is not built by treating each row as an independent Bernoulli trial; it is built by a cluster bootstrap that resamples game_id with replacement 1,000 times, re-bins the resampled rows, and reports the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the resulting gap distribution. A bin is only reported once its games clear a floor of 5 (min_games_per_bin_floor).

Why rows inside one game are not independent: the game's final outcome is fixed and terminal from the first row to the last. Both the model and the market probability path converge toward that one fixed number over the course of the game, so each new row sits close to the row before it rather than arriving as a fresh draw from some underlying distribution. A bin that happens to catch a game during a long stretch near, say, 55 percent will collect many rows that all say roughly the same thing about that one game, not many independent votes.

rho is the per-series lag-1 autocorrelation from residual_autocorrelation.json, summarized per sport as a median across games. ess_ledger.json applies the AR(1) formula to get ESS_AR1, then separately anchors on the raw distinct-game count for the same corpus, and reports ess_anchor as whichever of the two is smaller. It labels the game count the conservative anchor: AR(1) is one specific dependence model, while the game count needs no model of the dependence structure at all, only the fact that no two games are the same draw.

The calibration-stability bootstrap works at the game level, not the row level: each of the 1,000 replicates draws a set of game_ids with replacement equal in size to the original game count, pulls every row belonging to each drawn game (so a resampled game contributes its full run of rows, correlated block intact), rebuilds the 10-bin reliability curve from that resampled row set, and records the resulting gap and mean_y per bin. The reported gap_ci and mean_y_ci are the 2.5/97.5 percentile band of that distribution (ci_pct), computed under seed 20260722 with 1,000 replicates (n_boot). Resampling whole games, rather than rows, is what keeps a bin's reported interval honest about how many independent chances the data actually had to look different.

blocks.text: Both sports land on the game count as the tighter anchor: the AR(1) approximation alone would already say MLB rows carry only about 761 independent equivalents (a 10.2x inflation, per infl_ar1) and soccer rows about 172 (a 7.2x inflation), but the distinct-game floor is smaller still in both cases -- 227 and 51 -- so it is the number ess_ledger.json actually anchors on. share_ge_0_9, the share of game series with autocorrelation at least 0.9, is 0.955 for MLB model-side and 0.8235 for soccer model-side, so the great majority of games in both corpora sit in the high-dependence regime rather than a minority of outliers driving the median.

market-side rows show the same pattern: MLB market median autocorrelation is 0.9799 (n_games 225, share_ge_0_9 0.9644) and soccer market median is 0.9489 (n_games 51, share_ge_0_9 0.8039). ess_ledger.json's rho_market figures (0.9799 for MLB, 0.9489 for soccer) match these, confirming the ESS ledger and the autocorrelation ledger describe the same underlying series.

blocks.note: calibration_stability.json sports.mlb.sides.model_prob.bins[].{bin_lo,bin_hi,n,n_games,gap,gap_ci,significant}; rows per game is n divided by n_games, a direct ratio of the two published columns

blocks.text: Rows per game ranges from about 33 to 95 across the 10 MLB bins, and it is not flat: the two middle bins (0.4-0.5 and 0.5-0.6) show 88 and 95 rows per game, roughly twice the 33-49 seen in the tail bins. Those middle bins also have more games behind them (167 and 186, against 118-146 in the tails), so their large n is partly more games and partly each game dwelling there longer -- a near-even game sits close to a toss-up probability for long stretches, generating many correlated rows from the same handful of games, while a bin near 0 or 1 is typically entered once a game is effectively decided and viewed only briefly per game. A bin's row count is therefore not a uniform unit across the table: the same n in two different bins can represent a different number of independent games.

Of MLB's 10 model-side bins, 4 have a 95 percent gap interval that excludes zero (n_significant_bins) and 6 fall within the noise the bootstrap itself allows (n_within_noise_bins); the market side shows 0 of 10 significant and 10 of 10 within noise, at a Brier of 0.206653 against the model side's 0.237684. International soccer shows a different balance: 8 of 10 model-side bins have an interval excluding zero and 2 fall within noise, with the market side at 6 of 10 significant and 4 within noise (Brier 0.142726 for market against 0.227887 for model). The soccer corpus is both smaller (51 games versus 227) and shows a lower per-game autocorrelation floor in its worst series (minimum 0.4695 model-side, against 0.4866 for MLB), so its bins are supported by fewer games and by a wider spread of within-game dependence.

sections.heading: Robustness and what would falsify this

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Effective sample size (ESS) is the number of independent observations that would carry the same information as the correlated row count actually observed. ess_ledger.json reports two: an AR(1)-model estimate (ESS_AR1) and a distinct-game anchor, taking the smaller as the conservative headline (ess_anchor).

items: Both sports land with the game-count anchor below the AR(1) estimate (227 versus 761 for MLB, 51 versus 172 for soccer), which is the direction the method expects: AR(1) only models first-order dependence of a path that is, by construction, more constrained than that (terminal and smooth for the whole game), so a model that captured more of that structure would only push the true ESS lower, never higher than the game count.
residual_autocorrelation.json explicitly skips a duplicate mlb_clean corpus as byte-identical to mlb, so the MLB row and game counts used above are not double-counting one source under two labels.

Floors bound both ledgers: residual_autocorrelation.json requires at least 10 rows and a minimum residual variance before a game's series counts at all (2 MLB and 0 soccer series were skipped as low_n on the model side, 3 more MLB series skipped as flat), and calibration_stability.json will not report a bin built from fewer than 5 games. Neither ledger is silently thinned by a handful of degenerate games.

share_ge_0_9 (share of games with lag-1 autocorrelation at least 0.9) is high on both sides of both sports -- 0.955 MLB model, 0.9644 MLB market, 0.8235 soccer model, 0.8039 soccer market -- so the high median is not a few extreme games pulling up an otherwise low typical value.

blocks.text: What would falsify the reading that n overstates independent support: if the rows-per-game ratio in table 2 were close to 1 across bins (each game visiting each bin at most once), or if the published lag-1 autocorrelation were near zero, then a row would behave like an independent draw and the raw n would already approximate the effective sample size. Neither condition holds in either corpus: rows per game run from 33 to 95 in the MLB bin table, and median autocorrelation sits at 0.96-0.98 model-side in both sports.

items: The AR(1) approximation is a first-order model of a residual path that ess_ledger.json itself describes as smooth and terminal-constant, a stronger structure than one lag coefficient fully captures; the true independent information could sit below 761 for MLB and 172 for soccer, which is exactly why the ledger reports the conservative game-count anchor rather than trusting ESS_AR1 alone.

The distinct-game anchor treats every game as equally informative regardless of how many bins it touches or how long it lingers in a state; it does not itself carry the rows-per-game variation shown in table 2, so two bins with the same n_games are not guaranteed to be equally well supported if one draws its rows from far longer within-game dwell times.

These three artifacts cover one MLB corpus (227 games) and one international-soccer corpus (51 games); no NBA or tennis autocorrelation or ESS ledger is cited here, so this reading does not extend to those sports without their own published artifact.

The cluster bootstrap in calibration_stability.json corrects the width of each bin's confidence interval by resampling games, but the point estimates themselves (mean_p, mean_y, gap) are still computed once over all rows; the bootstrap changes how much a reader should trust the gap, not how many rows fed the gap's own calculation.

The three artifacts are not dated from one pipeline run: residual_autocorrelation.json carries no as_of or generated_at field (date not published), ess_ledger.json is dated 2026-07-25, and calibration_stability.json is dated 2026-07-23.

sections.heading: How to read this on the site

blocks.text: The observation-dependence inspector (/analytics/observation-dependence) shows the full published within-game residual-autocorrelation distribution behind table 1 and the figure above, sport by sport and side by side. The calibration inspector (/analytics/calibration) shows the reliability bins themselves with their already-applied game-cluster interval; reading it next to the effective sample size finding (Effective sample size, artifact ess_ledger.json) is how the site itself sequences this question, since the calibration inspector's own prerequisite points a reader to the effective-sample-size finding before comparing published bins, and the observation-dependence inspector in turn points to state-reliability once repeated ticks are accounted for.

blocks.label: Caution
blocks.text: A bin's n counts rows, not evidence. Read n_games next to it, and treat the gap_ci -- built from a bootstrap that resamples whole games -- as the number that actually reflects how many independent chances the data had to come out differently.

limitations: The AR(1) approximation is a first-order model of a residual path that is smooth and terminal-constant, a stronger structure than one lag coefficient fully captures, so the true independent information could sit below the reported ESS_AR1 values.

The distinct-game anchor treats every game as equally informative regardless of how many bins it touches or how long it dwells in a state, so it does not itself capture the rows-per-game variation shown in the MLB bin table.
These artifacts cover one MLB corpus (227 games) and one international-soccer corpus (51 games); no NBA or tennis autocorrelation or effective-sample-size ledger is cited here.
The game-cluster bootstrap corrects the width of a bin's confidence interval, not the number of rows behind its point estimate (mean_p, mean_y, gap), which is still computed once over all rows.

The three artifacts carry different or absent dates (residual_autocorrelation.json: date not published; ess_ledger.json: 2026-07-25; calibration_stability.json: 2026-07-23), so they are not guaranteed to reflect one shared pipeline run.
